title: Engineering Drawing
description: Previous Year Questions and Practice Questions covering projection systems, first/third-angle projection, types of lines, dimensioning principles, scales, title block & lettering, and numerical problems — for GATE, ESE, SSC-JE and State AE/JE preparation.

questions.text: The two sub-methods adopted for projection technique, viz. Visual Ray Method and Vanishing Point Method, are for:
questions.expl: Perspective projection is constructed using either the Visual Ray Method or the Vanishing Point Method to show realistic depth.

questions.text: Which projection method is commonly used in engineering drawing?
questions.expl: Orthographic projection is the standard method for working/manufacturing drawings as it shows true shape and size.

questions.text: In engineering drawing, the method most commonly adopted for preparing working drawings is:
questions.expl: Working drawings need accurate, to-scale views, which orthographic projection provides.

questions.text: Which projection method produces views showing true dimensions of faces parallel to the plane?
questions.expl: Orthographic projection shows the true size and shape of any surface parallel to the plane of projection.

questions.text: Perspective projection is mainly used to represent:
questions.expl: Perspective projection mimics how the human eye sees objects, giving a realistic pictorial appearance.

questions.text: The visual ray method and vanishing point method are associated with:
questions.expl: Both methods are classical techniques for constructing perspective drawings.

questions.text: Which of the following projections is classified as an axonometric projection?
questions.expl: Isometric projection is a type of axonometric (pictorial) projection where all three axes are equally foreshortened.

questions.text: In orthographic projection, the projection rays are assumed to be:
questions.expl: Parallel projectors perpendicular to the plane give orthographic projection its distortion-free, true-size views.

questions.text: Which plane is used to obtain the front view of an object?
questions.expl: The front view (elevation) is projected onto the Vertical Plane (VP).

questions.text: Which view best shows the width and depth of an object?
questions.expl: The top view (plan) is projected on the horizontal plane and reveals the object's width and depth.

questions.text: The minimum number of views required to fully describe an object is usually:
questions.expl: Most objects require the front, top and side views (three views) for a complete description.

questions.text: Which projection gives the most realistic appearance of an object?
questions.expl: Perspective projection replicates how the eye perceives depth, making it the most realistic.

questions.text: In isometric projection, the angle between any two principal axes is:
questions.expl: In isometric projection, the three axes are drawn 120° apart from each other.

questions.text: Which projection method is least suitable for taking measurements directly?
questions.expl: Isometric drawings foreshorten dimensions, so true measurements can't be read directly off the drawing.

questions.text: The plane perpendicular to both HP and VP is known as:
questions.expl: The Profile Plane (PP) is perpendicular to both the horizontal and vertical planes and is used for side views.

questions.text: Which projection method uses only one view to represent three dimensions pictorially?
questions.expl: Axonometric (e.g., isometric) projections show all three dimensions in a single pictorial view.

questions.text: Which projection shows only one face of an object but represents three dimensions pictorially?
questions.expl: Axonometric projections combine multiple dimensions into a single pictorial view from one direction.

questions.text: Which view is projected on the profile plane?
questions.expl: The side view is obtained by projecting the object onto the profile plane.

questions.text: In orthographic projection, distortion is eliminated because projection rays are assumed to be:
questions.expl: Parallel projection rays ensure that shapes and sizes are reproduced without distortion.

questions.text: As per first-angle projection, the appearance of the right-side surface of the object is drawn:
options: On the right side of the front view
On the left side of the front view
On the top of the front view
questions.expl: In first-angle projection, the object lies between the observer and the plane, so views are reversed — the right-side view appears on the left of the front view.

questions.text: In first-angle projection, the object is assumed to be:
options: In the first quadrant and behind the projection plane
In the first quadrant and between observer and plane
In the third quadrant and behind the plane
In the fourth quadrant and between planes
questions.expl: First-angle projection places the object in the first quadrant, between the observer and the projection plane.

questions.text: In first-angle projection, the top view of an object is drawn:
options: To the right of the front view
To the left of the front view
questions.expl: In first-angle projection, the top view is projected downward onto the horizontal plane and placed below the front view.

questions.text: In first-angle projection, the right-side view of an object is placed:
options: On the right of the front view
On the left of the front view
questions.expl: Because the object sits between observer and plane, the right-side view is projected onto the left-hand plane.

questions.text: Which projection system is officially recommended in India for engineering drawings?
questions.expl: Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) recommends first-angle projection for engineering drawings in India.

questions.text: The symbol of first-angle projection consists of:
options: Two truncated cones with larger end on right
Two truncated cones with larger end on left
questions.expl: The first-angle projection symbol shows two truncated cones (frustums) with the larger diameter end on the left.

questions.text: In third-angle projection, the object is assumed to be placed in:
questions.expl: Third-angle projection places the object in the third quadrant, behind the plane of projection.

questions.text: In first-angle projection, the observer is assumed to be positioned:
questions.expl: The observer is assumed to be at infinity, viewing through the object onto the plane behind it.

questions.text: In first-angle projection, the apparent reversal of views occurs because:
options: Observer is between plane and object
Object is between observer and plane
questions.expl: With the object between the observer and the plane, each view gets projected onto the far side, reversing the arrangement.

questions.text: Which projection system places views on the same side as the actual feature?
questions.expl: In third-angle projection, the plane lies between the observer and the object, so views appear on the same side as the feature they represent.

questions.text: In first-angle projection, why does the top view appear below the front view?
options: Due to downward rotation of HP
questions.expl: The horizontal plane is rotated downward (about the reference line) to bring it into the same plane as the vertical plane, placing the top view below.

questions.text: Which projection system is identified by the symbol where the larger end of the frustum is on the left?
questions.expl: This is the standard symbol for first-angle projection (as opposed to third-angle, where the larger end is on the right).

questions.text: Which feature distinguishes first-angle and third-angle projections most clearly?
questions.expl: The key difference lies in how the views are arranged relative to the front view, not in the object or sheet itself.

questions.text: The hidden lines in engineering drawing are used to represent:
questions.expl: Hidden (dashed) lines depict edges and surfaces that are not visible from the current viewing direction.

questions.text: Which line is used to indicate the limits of a dimension?
questions.expl: Extension lines project from the object outline to mark the limits within which the dimension line and value apply.

questions.text: Dimension lines are represented by:
questions.expl: Dimension lines are drawn thin and continuous, terminated with arrowheads at each end.

questions.text: Which of the following lines represents invisible edges of an object?
questions.expl: Hidden lines (short dashes) represent edges that are not visible in the given view.

questions.text: Which line is used to indicate the axis of symmetry of an object?
questions.expl: Center lines (thin chain/long-short dashed lines) mark axes of symmetry and centers of circles.

questions.text: Which line should never be used as a dimension line?
questions.expl: A center line should never be used directly as, or extended to serve as, a dimension line.

questions.text: Which line is used to indicate cutting planes in sectional views?
questions.expl: A cutting plane line (thick chain line with arrows) shows where an imaginary cut is made to create a section view.

questions.text: Object outlines in an engineering drawing are drawn using:
questions.expl: Visible object outlines are drawn as thick continuous lines so they stand out clearly.

questions.text: Center lines are represented by:
questions.expl: Center lines are thin chain lines — alternating long and short dashes.

questions.text: Which line type is used for dimensioning and extension lines?
questions.expl: Both dimension and extension lines are drawn as thin continuous lines to avoid visual dominance over the object outline.

questions.text: The conventional symbol for a center of a circle is:
questions.expl: The center of a circle is marked with two short crossed thin (center) lines.

questions.text: Which line type should be avoided for dimensioning purposes?
questions.expl: Center lines should not double as dimension lines since it can create ambiguity in the drawing.

questions.text: Which convention is used to represent materials like steel, brick, and concrete in section views?
questions.expl: Hatching (section lining) patterns, standardized per material, indicate cut surfaces in sectional views.

questions.text: The spacing between section lines should be:
questions.expl: Hatching lines should be evenly spaced and proportionate to the drawing scale for clarity.

questions.text: Which line is used to show imaginary extension of a surface?
questions.expl: Phantom lines (long-short-short chain lines) show alternate positions or imaginary extensions of a feature.

questions.text: The conventional representation of threads in engineering drawing is done using:
options: Combination of thick and thin lines
questions.expl: Screw threads are conventionally shown using a combination of thick (crest) and thin (root) continuous lines.

questions.text: Which line is used to indicate the limits of a partial or interrupted view?
questions.expl: A break line (freehand zig-zag or wavy) marks where a partial view or interrupted section is shown.

questions.text: Which line thickness hierarchy is correct?
questions.expl: Object (outline) lines are thickest, hidden lines are medium thickness, and dimension lines are thinnest.

questions.text: Which of the following conventions is used to show symmetry in drawings?
questions.expl: Center lines mark axes of symmetry in symmetrical features.

questions.text: Which line type is drawn freehand and zig-zag in nature?
questions.expl: Break lines are drawn freehand in a zig-zag or wavy style to indicate a shortened or interrupted view.

questions.text: Which line is used to show axis of cylindrical objects?
questions.expl: The center line marks the longitudinal axis of cylindrical features such as shafts and holes.

questions.text: In sectional views, cutting plane lines are generally drawn as:
questions.expl: Cutting plane lines are thick chain lines terminated with arrows indicating the viewing direction.

questions.text: Which convention is used to represent materials in sectional views?
questions.expl: Hatching lines represent the material of the cut surface in a section view.

questions.text: Which line should never be dimensioned directly?
questions.expl: Hidden lines represent invisible features and should not be dimensioned directly; a section view is preferred instead.

questions.text: Which convention is used to shorten long uniform objects in drawings?
questions.expl: A break line is used to shorten the representation of long, uniform-section objects while preserving scale accuracy elsewhere.

questions.text: Which line type takes visual priority over all others?
questions.expl: When lines coincide, the visible object (outline) line always takes precedence over hidden, center, or dimension lines.

questions.text: Which convention prevents confusion between adjacent sectioned components?
questions.expl: Adjacent parts in an assembly section are hatched at different angles (or spacing) to visually distinguish them.

questions.text: Why are center lines extended slightly beyond the outline of a circle?
questions.expl: A short extension beyond the outline makes the axis/center location clearly identifiable.

questions.text: Which condition justifies the use of break lines?
questions.expl: Break lines are used to shorten the drawn length of long objects that have a uniform cross-section throughout.

questions.text: The principal reason hidden lines are minimized in drawings is to:
questions.expl: Excessive hidden lines clutter a drawing; minimizing them (often via sections) keeps the drawing clear and readable.

questions.text: Why are section views preferred over hidden lines in complex drawings?
questions.expl: Sections replace confusing clusters of hidden lines with clear, visible internal detail.

questions.text: Which line type must dominate visually in a drawing?
questions.expl: The object (outline) line, being the thickest, should visually dominate over all other line types.

questions.text: The length-to-height ratio of a closed filled arrowhead is:
questions.expl: As per drawing standards, a closed filled arrowhead has a length-to-height (width) ratio of 3:1.

questions.text: The recommended ratio of length to width of a closed filled arrowhead is:
questions.expl: Same standard as above — arrowhead length should be three times its width.

questions.text: The main purpose of dimensioning in an engineering drawing is to:
options: Provide complete size and location information
questions.expl: Dimensioning conveys exact size and position information needed to manufacture the part without ambiguity.

questions.text: Which system of dimensioning places all dimension figures horizontally, readable from the bottom of the drawing?
questions.expl: In the unidirectional system, all figures are written horizontally so they can always be read from the bottom of the sheet.

questions.text: In the aligned system of dimensioning, dimension figures are:
options: Written parallel to the dimension line
questions.expl: In the aligned system, figures are oriented parallel to their dimension line so they read along its direction.

questions.text: As per standard practice, arrowheads used in dimensioning should be:
questions.expl: Standard practice recommends closed and filled arrowheads for clear, unambiguous termination of dimension lines.

questions.text: As per standard rules, dimension lines should generally be placed:
questions.expl: Dimension lines are conventionally kept outside the object outline to avoid cluttering the view.

questions.text: Which of the following should be avoided in dimensioning practice?
questions.expl: Duplicate dimensions can cause confusion or conflicting information and must be avoided.

questions.text: The numerical value of a dimension represents:
questions.expl: Dimension figures always state the true (actual) size of the object, regardless of the drawing scale used.

questions.text: Arrowheads should touch which element directly?
questions.expl: Arrowheads are placed at the ends of the dimension line, touching the extension lines that mark its limits.

questions.text: Which dimensioning method measures successive features from one reference surface?
questions.expl: Baseline (parallel) dimensioning measures every feature from a single common datum surface.

questions.text: Chain dimensioning is mainly used when:
questions.expl: Chain dimensioning links dimensions end-to-end; it's suitable only when overall accumulated length isn't critical, since tolerances add up.

questions.text: Extension lines should extend beyond the dimension line by approximately:
questions.expl: Standard practice extends extension lines about 2 mm past the dimension line arrowhead.

questions.text: Which rule must be followed while dimensioning holes?
questions.expl: Holes (full circles) are dimensioned using the diameter symbol (∅).

questions.text: Which dimensioning method minimizes accumulation of errors?
questions.expl: Baseline dimensioning references all dimensions to one datum, preventing tolerance stack-up seen in chain dimensioning.

questions.text: Which feature must never be dimensioned directly?
questions.expl: Hidden edges should not be dimensioned directly; a section or additional view should reveal them as visible edges first.

questions.text: Which rule is violated if the same dimension appears in two different views?
questions.expl: Repeating a dimension across views breaks the non-duplication rule and risks conflicting values after revisions.

questions.text: In dimensioning, arrowheads are preferred over dots because arrowheads:
questions.expl: Arrowheads give an unambiguous, sharply defined termination point for a dimension line.

questions.text: Which drawing element ensures interchangeability of manufactured parts?
questions.expl: Accurate dimensioning within specified tolerances is what allows parts made separately to fit together (interchangeability).

questions.text: Which dimensioning approach is most suitable when positional accuracy relative to a datum is critical?
questions.expl: Baseline dimensioning ties every feature's position directly to the datum, preserving positional accuracy.

questions.text: Which drawing element directly supports interchangeability?
questions.expl: As with Q20, correctly toleranced dimensions are what make interchangeable manufacturing possible.

questions.text: Which convention ensures that dimensions are independent of drawing scale?
questions.expl: Because the numerical value always states true size, dimensions remain valid regardless of how the drawing is scaled or reproduced.

questions.text: Which view is least suitable for dimension placement?
questions.expl: Perspective views are foreshortened/distorted pictorially, so they are unsuitable for placing accurate dimensions.

questions.text: Which drawing principle minimizes interpretation errors?
questions.expl: Providing only the necessary dimensions, clearly placed, reduces the chance of misreading or conflicting information.

questions.text: Which line type must never cross dimension figures?
questions.expl: The dimension line itself is conventionally broken/gapped where the numeral is written so no line passes through the figure.

questions.text: Which view should contain the maximum number of dimensions?
questions.expl: The front view, being the most descriptive view of an object, is generally used to carry the majority of dimensions.

questions.text: Which view arrangement helps reduce total number of dimensions?
questions.expl: Aligning related views logically lets dimensions be shared/referenced rather than repeated.

questions.text: Which principle ensures that a drawing can be interpreted without referring to written instructions?
questions.expl: A fully and correctly dimensioned drawing is self-explanatory and needs no supplementary text instructions.

questions.text: Which dimensioning practice best prevents tolerance accumulation?
questions.expl: Baseline dimensioning avoids the cumulative tolerance build-up inherent in chain dimensioning.

questions.text: Which statement regarding dimension values is correct?
questions.expl: Dimension figures always represent the true (actual) size of the object, never the scaled drawing length.

questions.text: Which view arrangement reduces repetition of dimensions?
questions.expl: Logically aligned views let a single dimension serve multiple related features, reducing repetition.

questions.text: Which feature should never be dimensioned directly?
questions.expl: As before, hidden edges should be revealed as visible (e.g. via a section) before being dimensioned.

questions.text: Which line should not cross dimension numerals?
questions.expl: The dimension line is broken at the numeral so the figure remains clearly legible.

questions.text: The customized plain scales in an engineering drawing are used to measure which one of the following?
options: Fraction of a main scale division
questions.expl: A plain scale can measure two consecutive units of length, e.g. meters and decimeters.

questions.text: The unit divided into equal parts on the right side of zero in a plain scale represents:
questions.expl: On a plain scale, the primary division to the right of zero represents the main units of measurement.

questions.text: Which scale is used to measure two successive units?
questions.expl: The plain scale is specifically designed to measure two successive units, e.g. meters and decimeters.

questions.text: Diagonal scale is mainly used to measure:
questions.expl: A diagonal scale can measure three consecutive units (e.g. meters, decimeters, centimeters) using similar triangles.

questions.text: The smallest division measured using a diagonal scale is obtained by:
questions.expl: The finest subdivision on a diagonal scale is read at the intersection point of the diagonal lines with horizontal divisions.

questions.text: Which scale is suitable for showing two different unit systems on the same drawing?
questions.expl: A comparative scale shows two different unit systems (e.g. km and miles) side by side for the same RF.

questions.text: In construction of scales, the length of scale is calculated using:
questions.expl: Length of scale = Maximum actual length to be represented × Representative Fraction (RF).

questions.text: The zero mark in a plain scale is placed:
questions.expl: Zero is placed between the main unit divisions (to the right) and sub-unit divisions (to the left).

questions.text: Which scale cannot measure fractions smaller than its smallest main division?
questions.expl: A plain scale is limited to reading whole sub-divisions and cannot resolve finer fractions like a diagonal scale can.

questions.text: Diagonal scale construction is based on the principle of:
questions.expl: Diagonal scales use the geometric principle of similar triangles to subdivide a unit accurately.

questions.text: Which scale is most suitable when high precision of small dimensions is required?
questions.expl: The diagonal scale allows accurate measurement of very small fractional units, unlike a plain scale.

questions.text: The maximum length represented by a scale is known as:
questions.expl: The term 'length of scale' refers to the total physical length representing the maximum measurable distance.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a requirement while selecting a scale?
questions.expl: The number of views on a sheet doesn't influence the choice of scale — sheet size, maximum dimension, and required accuracy do.

questions.text: In a diagonal scale, the vertical lines are divided to represent:
questions.expl: The vertical divisions on a diagonal scale mark the sub-units of the main scale.

questions.text: Which scale is rarely required in PSSSB JE examinations?
questions.expl: Comparative scales appear far less frequently than plain and diagonal scales in this exam pattern.

questions.text: Before constructing any scale, the first step is to:
questions.expl: Every scale construction begins by determining the RF and the maximum length to be represented.

questions.text: The primary purpose of using a scale in engineering drawing is to:
options: Represent large objects on smaller sheets accurately
questions.expl: Scales allow large (or very small) real-world objects to be represented proportionally and accurately on a standard sheet.

questions.text: Representative Fraction (RF) is defined as:
options: Ratio of drawing length to actual length in same units
Ratio of actual length to drawing length
Ratio of scale length to paper size
Ratio of paper size to drawing size
questions.expl: RF = Length on drawing ÷ Corresponding actual length, both measured in the same units.

questions.text: If RF of a scale is 1/50, it is known as:
questions.expl: An RF less than 1 (like 1/50) means the drawing is smaller than actual size — a reducing scale.

questions.text: If the RF of a scale is 2:1, the scale is classified as:
questions.expl: An RF greater than 1 means the drawing is larger than the actual object — an enlarging scale.

questions.text: If RF is greater than unity, the scale is classified as:
questions.expl: RF > 1 always indicates the object is being drawn larger than actual size (enlarging scale).

questions.text: The scale in which RF equals 1 is called:
questions.expl: When RF = 1, the drawing length equals the actual length — a full size scale.

questions.text: A plain scale can measure a maximum of:
questions.expl: By definition, a plain scale is limited to two consecutive units (e.g. meters and decimeters).

questions.text: If the smallest division required is 0.01 m, which scale is most appropriate?
questions.expl: Resolving such a fine subdivision accurately requires a diagonal scale's similar-triangle construction.

questions.text: A diagonal scale shows meters, decimeters, and centimeters. This implies it measures:
questions.expl: Three consecutive units being shown confirms this is a diagonal scale by definition.

questions.text: Which scale is constructed when fractional accuracy beyond one unit is required?
questions.expl: The diagonal scale is specifically used when finer fractional accuracy beyond a simple unit is needed.

questions.text: Why are diagonals used in diagonal scales?
questions.expl: Diagonal lines use similar triangles to precisely subdivide the smallest main division into finer parts.

questions.text: Which scale is mandatory when accuracy beyond one subdivision is required?
questions.expl: As above, a diagonal scale is required whenever precision finer than a simple subdivision is necessary.

questions.text: Why are diagonals drawn in a diagonal scale?
options: To subdivide the smallest unit accurately
questions.expl: Same principle — diagonals allow accurate subdivision of the smallest main unit using similar triangles.

questions.text: Which scale type is unsuitable for fractional measurement?
questions.expl: A plain scale cannot resolve fine fractional measurements the way a diagonal or vernier scale can.

questions.text: Which factor primarily governs scale selection?
questions.expl: The available drawing sheet size, relative to the object's actual dimensions, primarily determines the scale chosen.

questions.text: Which scale type is least likely to be asked directly in PSSSB JE?
questions.expl: Comparative scale questions appear far less often than plain, diagonal, or full-size scale questions in this exam.

questions.text: An object of length 10 m is drawn using a scale of RF = 1/50. The length of the drawing will be:
questions.expl: Drawing length = Actual length × RF = 1000 cm × (1/50) = 20 cm.

questions.text: If a 5 cm drawing represents an actual length of 2 m, the RF is:
questions.expl: RF = Drawing length ÷ Actual length = 5 cm ÷ 200 cm = 1/40.

questions.text: The length of a diagonal scale required to represent 5 m at RF 1/25 is:
questions.expl: Length of scale = Actual length × RF = 500 cm × (1/25) = 20 cm.

questions.text: In isometric projection, if true length is 50 mm, the isometric length will be approximately:
questions.expl: Isometric length = True length × 0.816 (isometric reduction factor) ≈ 50 × 0.816 ≈ 40.8 mm, closest to 45 mm among the options.

questions.text: A drawing uses RF = 1. If actual length is 80 mm, drawing length will be:
questions.expl: When RF = 1 (full-size scale), drawing length equals actual length exactly: 80 mm.

questions.text: If an object is reduced to one-tenth of its actual size, RF equals:
questions.expl: Reducing an object to one-tenth its size directly gives an RF of 1/10.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a title block in an engineering drawing?
options: To provide information about the materials used
To indicate the scale of the drawing
To show the date of creation
To display essential information about the drawing, such as the title, scale and author
questions.expl: The title block consolidates all key identifying information — title, scale, author, date, drawing number — in one place.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes a title block?
questions.expl: The title block functions as the drawing's information/identification panel.

questions.text: Which information is normally included in a title block?
questions.expl: Standard title blocks include the drawing title, scale used, and the author/drafter's name, among other details.

questions.text: Which of the following is a standard location for the title block?
questions.expl: By convention, the title block is placed in the bottom right corner of the drawing sheet.

questions.text: Which of the following information is NOT mandatory in a title block?
questions.expl: Sheet color has no bearing on the drawing's technical content and is not part of standard title block requirements.

questions.text: The main function of a title block is to:
questions.expl: The title block's core purpose is to give unique identification and reference data for the drawing.

questions.text: Which drawing element ensures traceability of revisions?
questions.expl: The title block typically includes a revision history/number, allowing changes to be tracked over time.

questions.text: Which information is essential for traceability of a drawing?
questions.expl: The unique drawing number in the title block is what allows a specific drawing to be traced and referenced.

questions.text: Which element of drawing is primarily responsible for legal documentation?
questions.expl: The title block carries the authorship, approval, and revision data that give the drawing formal/legal standing.

questions.text: In engineering drawing, lettering is mainly standardized to ensure:
questions.expl: Standardized lettering styles ensure that text on drawings is consistently legible to anyone reading it.

questions.text: Which type of lettering is most commonly recommended in engineering drawings?
questions.expl: Single-stroke Gothic vertical lettering is the style most commonly recommended for engineering drawings.

questions.text: The height of letters in engineering drawing is generally measured in:
questions.expl: Standard lettering heights (e.g. 2.5 mm, 3.5 mm, 5 mm) are specified in millimeters.

questions.text: Which symbol is used to indicate surface roughness?
questions.expl: A tick-shaped symbol is the standard convention used to indicate surface roughness/finish requirements.

questions.text: Which symbol is used to indicate surface roughness in drawings?
questions.expl: Same convention repeated — the tick symbol denotes surface finish/roughness value.

questions.text: Which lettering characteristic is most critical for dimensions?
questions.expl: Consistent, uniform letter height across all dimensions keeps the drawing legible and professional.

questions.text: Which lettering property most affects legibility of dimensions?
questions.expl: As above, uniform height is the single most important factor for legible dimension figures.

questions.text: Which characteristic defines good engineering lettering?
questions.expl: Good engineering lettering uses uniform, single-stroke thickness for clarity — never decorative variation.

questions.text: Which drawing error is most critical in production?
questions.expl: An incorrect dimension directly causes a manufacturing/production error, making it the most critical mistake.

questions.text: Which drawing error is least acceptable in competitive exams?
questions.expl: A conceptual error, like using the wrong projection system, reflects a fundamental misunderstanding and is least acceptable.

questions.text: Consider the following statements: (1) The horizontal angle measured clockwise from the geographic meridian to the direction of a line is known as Azimuth. (2) A line drawn through points of the same magnetic direction is called an Isogonic line. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.expl: Statement 1 correctly defines Azimuth. Statement 2 is incorrect — an isogonic line actually joins points of equal magnetic declination, not merely 'same direction'.

questions.text: Which statement best defines the fundamental objective of engineering drawing standards?
questions.expl: Drawing standards (like BIS/ISO) exist so that any engineer, anywhere, interprets a drawing the same way.

questions.text: Which statement best defines engineering drawing?
questions.expl: Engineering drawing is essentially a precise graphical language used by engineers to communicate design intent.

questions.text: Which statement best summarizes the role of engineering drawing in engineering practice?
questions.expl: Engineering drawing is a core, indispensable medium of technical communication in engineering practice.

questions.text: Which statement best describes engineering drawing?
questions.expl: As above, engineering drawing functions as a standardized technical communication language.

questions.text: Which convention ensures correct interpretation regardless of language?
questions.expl: Standardized symbols and conventions are universally understood, removing dependence on any spoken/written language.

questions.text: Which convention improves communication between designer and manufacturer?
questions.expl: Standard symbols ensure the manufacturer interprets the designer's intent exactly as specified.

questions.text: Which convention improves speed of drawing interpretation?
questions.expl: Familiar, standardized symbols can be recognized and interpreted quickly by any trained reader.

questions.text: Which factor does NOT influence the choice of projection method?
questions.expl: Sheet color is irrelevant to choosing between orthographic, isometric, or perspective projection.
